reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: The most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia; typically presents after the age of 60 with a male and ex-smoker predominance.
Progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough with bibasal fine end-inspiratory 'Velcro' crackles and finger clubbing are characteristic.

Diagnosis rests on a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern on HRCT: subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, and absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis.
Multidisciplinary team discussion integrating clinical, radiological and, where required, histological data is the diagnostic reference standard.
Antifibrotic therapy slows the decline in forced vital capacity but does not reverse established fibrosis.
Acute exacerbations, defined by rapid worsening with new ground-glass change over fibrosis, carry a very high mortality.
Actively screen for and manage comorbidities: gastro-oesophageal reflux, pulmonary hypertension, coexisting emphysema, obstructive sleep apnoea and lung cancer.
Refer eligible patients early for lung transplantation assessment and for pulmonary rehabilitation and palliative symptom support.
reference.pathophysiology: Repetitive micro-injury to ageing alveolar epithelium in genetically susceptible individuals provokes aberrant wound healing rather than a primarily inflammatory response. Dysregulated epithelial-fibroblast crosstalk drives fibroblast and myofibroblast proliferation with excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing fibroblastic foci, irreversible architectural distortion and honeycombing that is subpleural and basal in distribution. Telomere-related and surfactant protein gene variants and the MUC5B promoter polymorphism contribute to disease susceptibility.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (notably rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis)
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax with supine and prone acquisitions to identify a UIP pattern
Full pulmonary function tests including transfer factor (restrictive defect with reduced DLCO)
Autoimmune serology (antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, myositis panel) to exclude connective tissue disease
Serum precipitins and a detailed environmental and occupational exposure history
Six-minute walk test with oximetry to document exertional desaturation
Surgical or transbronchial lung cryobiopsy when the HRCT pattern is indeterminate and the multidisciplinary team advises
Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Rapidly worsening breathlessness with new widespread ground-glass change over fibrosis suggesting an acute exacerbation
Clinical signs of right heart failure or pulmonary hypertension
Haemoptysis or a new pulmonary mass raising concern for lung cancer
Rapid decline in forced vital capacity
reference.prognosis: Median survival has historically been three to five years from diagnosis, although the course is highly variable and antifibrotic therapy slows progression. Acute exacerbations and progressive respiratory failure are the leading causes of death.
pitfalls: Mislabelling fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis or connective tissue disease-ILD as IPF and missing a treatable or removable cause
Attributing crackles and breathlessness to cardiac disease and delaying HRCT
Using combination immunosuppression as for other interstitial pneumonias, which is harmful in IPF
Overlooking coexisting pulmonary hypertension, emphysema or lung cancer
Failing to discuss transplantation and palliative symptom control early
